title: Tunes played and bands competing on Sundays
summary: He cannot recall the tune names, mentions Scott Joplin music, and describes bands showing off for club crowds on Sundays.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: What tunes would they play back in those times?

Oh, man, I'll be frank with you, I had to go back some to get them together. But, uh, it was a great deal of Scott Junkins' music. Yeah, they played lots of that stuff, man. I don't think I'd know it for him. While I holler and, uh, blaming on the blues and physical defeat. Oh, man, that's a gang of stuff. Oh, good minutes. Stuff that I just don't know the name of. But that was the most of the music, though, they never played no, uh, make-up numbers, you know? Mm-hmm. That was all solid stuff. High Society, Maryland, and some of that stuff we used to play there, and I don't think I could do anything with it, just direct. Yeah. Do you remember Walla Holla?
I don't believe I'm in Hummerwood or anything. I don't know Walla Holla. Go with me. I haven't forgotten that thing again. Sounds like down home right down. Mm-hmm. Wow, I can't think of that.
All that stuff has got away from me, man.
I'm playing with these different men that's come along, you know? They pick up, and you come down and something works while it's different.
Well, in that time, you see, that was hard and usually. You see, you get a band, you take a link to a day like on a Sunday, or you catch every

band in town. You see, to have work, you have to have a band, you have to have a band, and you have to have a band. But on the Sundays, you catch them big clubs, they get on out there and they watch for the bands. They get to have their band. They get to have their band. They get to have their band. They get out there and they watch, stand up and watch what band's coming along. The band gets the hot with you on one number, it's carrying your numbers. Well what you do, you go back and what you call the Red Bull, pick one of them old hard numbers off, you throw him off, you see. When you throw him off he'll get neat, you'll get behind him and you wham up. That's where we used to figure it out. But now it's so much different in the music now, I don't know man. There ain't much in the music now. Nobody's playing, it's hard to get a bunch of men together to play music. They ain't going to play the right stuff, they're going to upset all the stuff you've got, they can play it their way. You understand? I understand many bands playing, they tell you it's their number and all that, and you come to find out the peak number come here, some off of this number, some off of that number, some off the other number. Well the majority of them that knew it is gone, so what they're going to do to get them by with? Really if you was to take a bunch of men, pick up a bunch of old time men and get back on their music men like, like you say for instance like Charl and them men that got that stuff and Pete and that, man you'll get back on that stuff man, you'll demand a job. What I mean by demand a job, you want to study how to play it, you wouldn't want to be mixed up here with what you hear now. Because what you hear now ain't but, you can see it's three tunes. Take all that playing right now, ain't but three numbers. You can always put a different tone to it, a different temper to it, or something, you know, put to it to make a sound, but it's the same thing over and over and over. For instance you take one of them and put it right there and start to play it and now you'll get tired of it. You'll get the next one the same thing. Take all these bands here, these old men here, they got some pretty good music they can play there. That music here there's nobody using. You might hear from those big crack shots, you know what I'm saying, you hear them play. You ain't going to hear these, for instance, like you see the bands playing up with one or two hundred men in the band, they're playing that stuff out here with your head and we used to play that stuff with four and five men. You take a climb, they'll land some man, a trumpet, he'll land some maybe a trombone, and he's all around there and he's filling all them little gaps that's left open. Now just direct climb it. Now I tell you now, climb it. Go climb it, nowhere else. Go get there, go bass. Go that one way before man, if you miss you on, man, somebody ride in there on you until you're able to come back. That's different in the music. You never went back and disfigured that, right? I see when we did have the Young Imperial Band, we was out in Charleston, Louisiana, we met, we met, uh, uh, Clayborne Williams out there and we were waiting for a fellow Mr. Roberts and Mr. Settlers. And he told us about, uh, Sharpen Up, because Clayborne Williams had a pretty tough band and he was well liking out there. Well we had a pretty good band. I said, I'm not criticizing your band and nothing, they say, but he's well liking. You know when people like you, they're always going to give you right when you're wrong. Well we didn't sharpen up for him, man. We did. We went back and all that old stuff with Scots music and sharpen up. And the first thing we met him was with high society and high society, dressing, juice, frizzy, the feet and all that stuff would come up there. But when the big thing come off, we had it. He come out with a whole lot of heavy marches and things and heavier bands, but that didn't get it because we was cutting in there with dance music, you see, and, well you see, a few types of dance music and march music. Well he come in with march music. He had one point, we took the three points and gave it to us. We sharpened up on everything they had then, we had a good band. Two of the bands. Barbarin, John Marrero, and, uh, Artemis Don's bass. Let's see, and, Barley called George, we called him Kalkai George. That's the only thing I know about George. He was, uh, he was King the Turca. We had Ambrose, Powers, Wooden Joe. We had Wooden Joe, well, uh, and Ambrose, yeah, Wooden Joe Ambrose. And who else was there? T-Bar, uh, Barbarin. That's the band we had. Well, it was Wooden Joe playing then.
